label: Approaching, not achieved
rationale: Every 2025 estimate published in 26H1 is a new record: GCB fossil CO2 38.1 GtCO2 (+1.0%), IEA energy CO2 38,082 MtCO2 (+0.4%) and Carbon Monitor fossil+industry CO2 37.2 GtCO2 (+0.7%); only GCB total CO2 dipped slightly, due to lower land-use emissions as El Niño ended. Growth has slowed to a plateau (global fossil power generation fell 0.2%, China and India flat), but China's CO2 rose 2% in Q1 2026 and the IEA expects the shock-driven 2026 oil-demand fall to rebound above the 2025 level in 2027, so the peak is not definitively behind us. Caveat: the milestone covers all greenhouse gases, but no global 2025 total-GHG estimate was published within 26H1, so CO2 estimates serve as the proxy.

label: Worsening
rationale: The Mauna Loa CO2 concentration hit new records in 26H1: a 432.34 ppm monthly mean in May 2026 (+1.83 ppm on May 2025) and a 433.95 ppm daily mean on 1 May. The 10-year trend (NOAA Jan->Dec, 2016-2025) is 2.56 ppm/yr at MLO (2.53 global); its dip from 2.64 is mechanical (El Niño year 2015 left the window) and half-decade means still rose (2.51 -> 2.61 ppm/yr), so there is no structural slowdown. Year-on-year growth temporarily slowed (+1.48 to +2.26 ppm in Jan-Jun 2026), matching in direction the Met Office forecast of a slower 2026 annual-mean rise that it attributes to La Niña-like conditions, but it remains far above the 1.33-1.79 ppm/yr that IPCC 1.5°C pathways require.

label: Approaching, not yet achieved
rationale: Global fossil CO2 emissions still rose to a record 38.1 GtCO2 in 2025 (+1.1%), so the peak has not been reached. China (32% of global emissions) has been flat or falling for 18 months, driven by clean energy, which may mark the beginning of the end.

label: Distant — 53 GtCO2e/year to eliminate
rationale: Global GHG emissions were 53.2 GtCO2e in 2024 and fossil CO2 hit a record in 2025, far from net zero. Net-zero targets cover 77% of global GDP, but 2025 was a year of retreat (US Paris withdrawal, banks exiting NZBA, delayed corporate targets) and most IEA net-zero pathway benchmarks are off track.

label: Under pressure
rationale: 2024 was the first calendar year to exceed 1.5°C above pre-industrial (WMO 1.55°C), though the long-term Paris metric remains ~1.3-1.4°C. WMO gives 70% odds the 2025-2029 average also exceeds 1.5°C, and the 1.5°C carbon budget is virtually exhausted.

label: ⚠️ Accelerating in the wrong direction
rationale: Atmospheric CO2 reached 426.5 ppm (Nov 2025) with the annual peak exceeding 430 ppm for the first time, and the 2023-2024 increase of +3.5 ppm was the largest on record. The jump was driven by continued fossil emissions, El Niño-weakened land sinks and record wildfires.

label: Distant — ~54 GtCO2e/year to eliminate
rationale: EDGAR 2026 put total greenhouse-gas emissions excluding LULUCF at 54.1 GtCO2e in 2025, up 0.7% on 2024, and GCB 2025 put total CO2 (fossil + land-use change) at a preliminary 42.2 GtCO2 in 2025, so net emissions remain nowhere near zero. At the 23 September 2026 UN Climate Summit, Guterres said emissions are still rising and a temporary 1.5°C overshoot is expected, calling for national fossil-fuel transition roadmaps, of which Germany's (23 September) is only the third after France and the Netherlands, while the US President attacked the IMO Net-Zero Framework for shipping ahead of its December 2026 adoption vote. Corporate commitments keep growing (700+ Climate Pledge signatories targeting net zero by 2040) but do not change the global picture.

label: Plateau, peak not confirmed
rationale: The total-GHG gap is now filled: EDGAR 2026 put greenhouse-gas emissions excluding LULUCF at 54.1 GtCO2e in 2025, up 0.7% on 2024, alongside record 2025 fossil CO2 (GCB 38.1 GtCO2, +1.0%; IEA energy CO2 38,082 MtCO2, +0.4%). For 2026, Climate TRACE estimates total GHG for January-July 0.3% above the same period of 2025, while Carbon Brief projects global fossil CO2 to fall about 0.5% in 2026, a decline driven by the Strait of Hormuz oil shock that the IEA expects to reverse in 2027 when oil demand rises above its 2025 level. China's CO2 remains below its 2023-24 peak (Q2 2026 -1%, H1 up marginally) but India's CO2 rose 3.7% in H1 2026, so the peak is still not definitively behind us.

label: Under growing pressure
rationale: Berkeley Earth (24 September 2026) put August 2026 at 1.71 ± 0.11°C above 1850-1900, the warmest August on record, and judged the 2026 annual mean 'all but certain' to exceed 1.5°C (likely 1.536-1.642°C) with a 93% chance of a record year, as a record-strength El Niño (daily Niño 3.4 anomaly 3.11°C on 21 September) is expected to add further warming in 2027. These are single-month and single-year anomalies; the latest long-term (Paris-metric) warming estimate in the ledger is WMO's ~1.3-1.4°C for 2024, so the 2°C ceiling has not been breached. However, the GCB puts the remaining 50% 1.5°C budget at 170 GtCO2 from 2026 (about 4 years at 2025 emissions) and emissions have not yet peaked, so holding peak warming below 2°C remains plausible but increasingly strained.

label: Worsening, El Niño spike ahead
rationale: After the record 432.34 ppm May 2026 monthly mean, NOAA Mauna Loa (MLO) monthly means fell seasonally to 429.13 ppm in July and 427.55 ppm in August 2026, still 1.26 and 2.07 ppm above the same months of 2025, so the concentration keeps rising and the July gain was only a continuation of the temporary 26H1 slowdown. The 10-year trend (NOAA Jan->Dec growth, 2016-2025) is unchanged at 2.56 ppm/yr at MLO (2.53 global), far above the 1.33-1.79 ppm/yr 2020s decadal average that the Met Office says IPCC 1.5°C scenarios require. New since July, Zeke Hausfather (28 September 2026) expects an El Niño-driven spike in the atmospheric CO2 growth rate in 2027, similar to the record 3.33 ppm MLO growth of 2024, as models put the 2026-27 El Niño's Niño 3.4 peak around 4.1°C; this is a qualitative projection, but it points to re-acceleration rather than relief, so the status stays red.

label: Regressing: 427.35 ppm (2025); 10-yr growth 2.56 vs 2.15 ppm/yr, need <=1.79 (tier 1)
rationale: The assessed quantity, the 10-year mean of NOAA Mauna Loa Jan->Dec CO2 growth, rose to 2.56 ppm/yr for 2016-2025 from 2.15 ppm/yr for the previous non-overlapping window 2006-2015 (+0.41, about 1.9 standard errors), and half-decade means rose monotonically (1.97, 2.34, 2.51, 2.61 ppm/yr), so the growth rate is moving away from the goal of <= 0. The tier-1 benchmark, a 2020s mean growth of at most 1.79 ppm/yr for IPCC C1 1.5°C pathways (Met Office), is far exceeded (2.61 ppm/yr for 2021-2025). The Jan-Jun 2026 year-on-year slowdown (+1.48 to +2.26 ppm) spans less than a window and has a named reversing cause (La Niña-like conditions), so it is discounted as a transient; the record 2025 annual mean of 427.35 ppm is reported, not scored.

label: Distant: net CO2 42.2 Gt (2025), ~53 GtCO2e GHG (2024), not yet falling; ETA >10 yrs
rationale: Net emissions are not yet declining: GCB puts total CO2 (fossil + land-use change) at 42.4 GtCO2 in 2024 and a preliminary 42.2 GtCO2 in 2025, with fossil CO2 at a record 38.1 GtCO2 (+1.0%), and total-CO2 growth only slowed to 0.3%/yr over 2015-2024. Extrapolating that trend gives no evidenced path to approximately zero within 10 years (the emissions peak itself is not yet behind us), so the ETA is over 10 years and the status is red. Net-zero targets covering 77% of global GDP are pledges, which cannot lift the status, while US Paris withdrawal (legacy record) is a policy obstacle rather than the determining block.

label: Distant: GHG 54.1 GtCO2e (2025, +0.7%), not yet falling; 9x cut + removals needed, ETA ~2090
rationale: Net GHG emissions (54.1 GtCO2e excl. LULUCF in 2025, +0.7%, plus ~4 GtCO2 net land use) have not started to fall, and reaching approximately zero needs a ~9x cut of gross emissions to a ~6 Gt residual balanced by removals. Extrapolating the measured deceleration of emission growth (0.08-0.14 percentage points per year, constant curvature) from a peak around 2030 gives net zero around 2082-2104, median ~2090, with discounted national pledges (2050-2070, GDP-weighted ~2075 after discount) as the early tail; Gt-scale removals are four orders of magnitude short and tech-CDR offtakes shrank in 2026. The median ETA is over 10 years, so the status is red; roadmaps and pledges are announcements or policy intentions that cannot lift it.

eta.method: trend (constant-curvature decline of emission growth, log space) from the-bend peak, with removals as structural floor; cross-checked against IPCC reference class and discounted proponent (pledge) dates
eta.calc: Gap: net GHG ~58 GtCO2e (54.1 excl. LULUCF 2025 + ~4.1 net LUC) to a ~6 Gt residual balanced by removals: 54.1/6 = 9x, ln 9 = 2.2. Growth rate falls 0.054-0.137 pp/yr per yr (co2-emissions-fossil-gcb decadal growth 2.27/1.73/0.93 %/yr for 1995-2005/2005-15/2015-25; co2-emissions-total-gcb 1.73/1.60/0.23), i.e. curvature a = 0.0008-0.0014/yr^2. Peak ~2030 (the-bend), then ln9 = a/2 t^2: t = sqrt(4.4/a) = 52 yr (a 0.0016, 2082), 61 yr (0.0012, 2091), 74 yr (0.0008, 2104). Ramp model: decline reaching 4 %/yr over 20 yr -> 2095; 6 %/yr over 16 yr -> 2075. Drivers: solar LCOE 417 -> 43 $/MWh 2010-2024, -15 %/yr (fusion lcoe-solar-pv-irena, legacy); renewable additions 666 GW 2024 -> 693 GW 2025 (+4 %); electricity 23 % of final energy, <30 % by 2035 on current policy; DAC ~0.01 Mt/yr vs ~10 Gt needed. Cross-checks: IPCC AR6 C1 net-zero GHG early 2070s, C3 ~2100+; pledges 2050/2060/2070 discounted 1.5x -> 2062/2077/2092 (~2075 GDP-weighted); Exxon 30 Gt energy CO2 in 2050 -> after 2100; prev v1 '>10 years' had no number. Working: eta-notes.md
eta.cruxes: Earlier: a confirmed global peak before 2030 followed by >1 %/yr declines; renewable additions back to 20 %+/yr growth; DACCS/BECCS offers turning into delivered Mt. Later: no peak by 2030 (2027 oil/El Niño rebound sets a new record), methane still rising, CDR offtakes keep shrinking, further US/IMO policy rollback.

eta.method: trend (linear decline of the growth rate, i.e. constant curvature in log space) on a CO2 proxy for GHG, plus a confirmation floor for 'definitively'; cross-checked with reference class (regional peaks) and discounted proponent dates
eta.calc: GHG (EDGAR) 54.1 GtCO2e 2025, growth +0.7 %/yr; target growth <= 0 then a confirmed decline. Proxy series: co2-emissions-fossil-gcb 23.26 (1995), 29.19 (2005), 34.71 (2015), 38.1 (2025): decadal growth 2.27 -> 1.73 -> 0.93 %/yr, deceleration 0.054 then 0.080 pp/yr per yr; co2-emissions-total-gcb 29.53/35.12/41.22/42.2: 1.73 -> 1.60 -> 0.23 %/yr, deceleration 0.137. Zero growth: 0.7/0.137 = 5.1 yr (2031) to 0.7/0.080 = 8.8 yr (2034); 0.7/0.054 = 13 yr (2038). Near term: 2026 ~flat/-0.5 % fossil (Hormuz shock, projection); 2027 oil +2 mb/d = 0.31 GtCO2 (+0.6 % of GHG) -> likely new record. Peak p50 ~2030 (fit 2031-2034, pulled earlier by China flat since Mar 2024 and Exxon's own outlook of 36 -> 30 Gt energy CO2 by 2050). Confirmation: 3 post-peak years are only a*9/2 = 0.4-0.6 % below the peak (inside revision noise); reaching -2 % takes sqrt(0.04/a) = 5.4-7.1 yr, ~3-4 yr with structural evidence; median lag ~5 yr incl. ~1 yr publication -> 2030 + 5 = 2035. Cross-checks: regional peaks (US 2007) were called definitive 4-8 yr later; China's Mar-2024 peak still 'open' after 21 months; IEA 'peak by mid-2020s' calls discounted 1.5-2x -> peak ~2027-2029; prev v1 band '5-10 years (~2031-2036)', median now inside it. Later: a 2027 global record above +1 %; China rebound (thermal capacity additions +20 %, solar additions -58 % Jan-Aug 2026); renewable additions stalling at ~700 GW; methane growth.

basis.path: Trend extrapolation on GCB CO2 as proxy for total GHG (CO2 is ~75 % of GHG and drives year-to-year changes; methane/N2O grow at a similar ~0.5-1 %/yr, so the peaks should be within a few years): growth decelerating ~0.1 pp/yr each year, China flat or falling since March 2024, global fossil power -0.2 % in 2025, clean power now covering demand growth. The 2026 fossil-CO2 dip is a shock-driven projection and does not count.

label: Distant: ~1.4°C long-term, rising; trend overshoots to ~2.4°C peak; ETA ~2080 if at all
rationale: Warming peaks only when net CO2 reaches zero, and long-term warming (~1.3-1.4°C, 2024; 1.48°C over the 12 months to August 2026) is still rising. On the emission trend (peak ~2030, then a decline accelerating by ~0.1%/yr each year) cumulative CO2 from 2026 is ~1500-2000 Gt against a ~1020 Gt median 2°C budget, so the trend peak is ~2.3-2.6°C and staying below 2°C needs a decline 3-4x faster than the trend or a low climate response (P ~25%). Conditional on achievement, warming peaks and is confirmed around 2065-2095 (median ~2080), with p90 open (maybe never), so the status is red.

basis.rule: Milestone red (RUBRIC.md v2 §4): median ETA over 10 years after made_at (basis.eta.p50 2080, conditional on achievement), and the trend path overshoots 2°C

eta.method: driver trend (cumulative CO2 on the extrapolated emission path x carbon budget/TCRE) plus structural floor (warming peaks at net-zero CO2, confirmed in the long-term mean); p10/p50 conditional on achievement, reference class IPCC AR6 pathways
eta.calc: Now ~1.3-1.4°C long-term (WMO 2024), 2024 annual 1.55°C, 12-mo to Aug 2026 1.48°C; target: peak < 2.0°C. 2°C (50 %) budget from 2026 = 170 Gt (GCB 1.5°C) + 850 Gt (AR6 1350-500 per +0.5°C) = 1020 GtCO2 = 24 yr of 42.2 Gt (co2-emissions-total-gcb 2025). Trend path: ~flat to 2030 (169 Gt) then constant-curvature decline a = 0.0008-0.0016/yr^2 (from GCB decadal growth 1.73/0.93 %/yr fossil, 1.60/0.23 total): cumulative = 169 + 42.2*sqrt(pi/2a) = 1491 (a 0.0016) / 1696 (0.0012) / 2039 Gt (0.0008) -> peak 1.5 + (C-170)*0.5/850 = 2.28 / 2.40 / 2.60°C. Staying < 2°C needs a ~0.0038 (7-8 %/yr decline 20 yr after peak). P(peak < 2°C) ~25 % (low-TCRE tail: 33rd-pct 2°C budget ~1450 Gt from 2026; faster transition; SRM, politically blocked). Unconditional median = not achieved, so p50 is the conditional median: fast branch net-zero CO2 2030 + sqrt(2 ln(42.2/5)/0.0038) = 2064, peak confirmed ~2070; low-response trend branch net-zero CO2 2030 + sqrt(2 ln 8.4/0.0012) = 2090, confirmed ~2095 -> median ~2080. Cross-checks: IPCC AR6 only C1-C3 (net-zero CO2 2050-2070s) keep < 2°C; KPI 2.56 ppm/yr vs <= 1.79 for C1; Exxon 30 Gt energy CO2 in 2050 implies > 2.5°C; prev v1 '>10 years' had no number and no budget check. Working: eta-notes.md
eta.cruxes: Earlier/more likely: a global emission peak before 2030 followed by > 3 %/yr declines in the 2030s; low-side revisions of TCRE/ECS; governed SRM research advancing. Later/less likely: the 2026-27 super El Niño pushing the long-term mean past 1.5°C early, aerosol unmasking, weakening land/ocean sinks (15 % weaker already), emissions still rising after 2030.

basis.path: Driver: the global CO2 emission trajectory (milestone:the-bend / the-balance) against the remaining carbon budget; warming ~0.25°C/decade would cross 2°C (long-term) around 2050 if emissions stay near 42 Gt. On the decelerating trend the peak is ~2.3-2.6°C, so the milestone needs a much faster decline than measured, a low climate response, or sunlight management.
blockers: Global emissions not yet peaked; GHG 54.1 GtCO2e in 2025 (+0.7 %), net CO2 ~42 GtCO2 (trend, physical/economic)
Carbon budget (physical): 2°C 50 % budget ~1020 GtCO2 from 2026 vs ~1500-2000 Gt cumulative on the trend; 1.5°C budget 170 Gt (~4 years)
